title: Comparing Five Loop Closure Variants
description: Test five comprehension and for-loop closure patterns to see which ones share a single loop variable and which create a fresh binding per iteration.
source: draft: agy free model + edit: codex

steps.description: Lines 1-2 define `factory(v)` returning `lambda: v`. Lines 6-8 build three list comprehensions over `range(3)`: `a` with a bare `lambda: i`, `b` with a default parameter `lambda i=i: i`, and `c` calling `factory(i)`.
Lines 9-15 build two `for i in range(3):` loops: `d` appends a bare `lambda: i` on each iteration (line 11), while `e` appends `factory(i)` on each iteration (line 14).

Compare `a` (line 6) and `d` (lines 10-11). Python gives a list comprehension its own scope separate from the module scope. All three iterations of `a` run inside that single comprehension scope, just as all three iterations of `d` run in the module scope.

steps.question: Before running lines 17-22, which of the five lists (`a`, `b`, `c`, `d`, `e`) print `[2, 2, 2]` and which print `[0, 1, 2]`?
steps.answer: `a` and `d` print `[2, 2, 2]` because their bare lambdas share one `i` binding across all three iterations. `b`, `c`, and `e` print `[0, 1, 2]`. The default argument `i=i` or `factory(i)` call creates a new binding on each iteration.

steps.description: Lines 17-22 call `[f() for f in fns]` on all five lists and print the results.
At trace step 11 while building `c`, `factory(0)` runs line 2 in a fresh call frame where `v = 0` and returns `lambda: v` bound to that frame.
